sql_runner.py:95 calls effective_row_cap(self._max_rows) in the coroutine on the caller's context. limits.py:36-54 reads get_effective_settings() and returns min(constructor_cap, effective.max_rows), or the constructor cap when none is bound. The same function with the same context gives the same value as a per-request read. The value is passed as `cap` into _run_sql_blocking (lines 98-139), so no contextvar read happens in the thread. _run_sql_blocking reads only self._read_only, self._statement_timeout_ms, self.database_path, sql and cap. It makes no get_effective_settings, read-only-profile or RLS calls, so no other per-request value needs a pre-read. asyncio.to_thread copies the context anyway, so the pre-read is explicit and not strictly required.

sql_runner.py:94-95 reads the cap via effective_row_cap (which calls get_effective_settings, limits.py:51) on the caller context, then passes the int to asyncio.to_thread. _run_sql_blocking (97-172) uses only self.pymysql/host/kwargs/_read_only/_statement_timeout_ms (plain instance attributes), pymysql connection and SSDictCursor/DictCursor, is_read_shaped (readonly.py:52, pure string check), rows_to_capped_df/mark_truncation (limits.py:30-72, pure pandas, no contextvar) and the module logger. No contextvar or event-loop-thread dependence in the thread body other than the pre-read cap. Hostile input considered: a per-request profile cap narrower than the constructor; it is read before the handoff, so the thread uses it correctly.

sql_runner.py:128 run_sql does only effective_row_cap then awaits asyncio.to_thread(self._run_sql_blocking, args.sql, cap). All driver work (connect :133/:135, set_session :148, cursor/execute/fetchmany :152-171, commit :189, close :206) is inside _run_sql_blocking. The connection is created, used and closed within that single worker-thread call, never shared across threads, so psycopg2 (threadsafety 2) is not stressed. The named cursor (uuid hex name :164, fetchmany(cap+1) :171, cursor.close in finally :172-183, conn.close in outer finally :198-208) has no loop-thread dependence. There is no explicit rollback call; conn.close() discards the open transaction, so the claim's 'rollback/cleanup' holds as cleanup.

Comment (sqlite/sql_runner.py:92-94) says the thread runs until the driver returns and that a *configured* statement timeout bounds it. All runners use asyncio.to_thread (sqlite:96, postgres:128, mysql:95), so a cancelled caller leaves the thread running. Timeout is applied only when statement_timeout_ms>0 (default 0 = disabled): sqlite progress-handler deadline at :125-129, postgres SET statement_timeout at postgres:151-156, mysql SET SESSION MAX_EXECUTION_TIME at mysql:119-126. Tested input: cancelled caller with statement_timeout_ms=0 has no bound, but the comment's 'configured' qualifier does not claim one there, so it does not falsify it. Minor nuance: MySQL MAX_EXECUTION_TIME only affects SELECTs (mysql:120), not worth a FAIL.

tests/unit/test_sql_runner_event_loop.py:28-48,78,94,110. Blocking sleep SLOW_S=0.4 s in connect or execute. A free loop runs the heartbeat every 0.02 s, which is about 20 ticks, against a threshold of 5. That is a 4x margin, so the average wake period would have to exceed 80 ms to fail. A blocked loop (driver called directly on the loop) never lets the heartbeat run during the sleep. The heartbeat is cancelled right after run_sql returns, so ticks stays 0 and the assertion fails. Hostile input considered: a loaded CI runner with coarse asyncio.sleep wakeups. Sustained 4x slippage is implausible, since time.sleep in a worker thread releases the GIL. This could not be run, so the non-flakiness rests on the margin reasoning, not on observed runs.
